Learn the basics

After the barge example and the methods in Sollied, A.J. (2009), Strukturdesign av skip, Høgskolen i Ålesund. For educational use only.

Structure from DBB

  1. Open a design saved by the Ship Design Building Block Editor (Save gives a .json file), or pick an example (the barge is the hand calculation of Sollied 2009: shear force 600 t and moment 9000 t m, to compare). The design needs one hull; the blocks below the main deck give the layout.
  2. The ship is split into regions at the transverse bulkheads found in the blocks: places where block ends meet across most of the breadth. Click a region in the side view or in the list.
  3. Each region gets one section at its middle, on the real hull shape. Inner bottom, inner side or longitudinal bulkhead and tween decks come from the blocks; the right panel says which blocks.
  4. Every structure is filled with plates and longitudinals at the spacing, and every fifth longitudinal is a primary member (in a double bottom, a side girder). Each is sized to the rules and checked; green is met, red is not met.
  5. Framing is guessed per region: transverse for ships under 60 m and for regions near the ends, longitudinal elsewhere. A transversely framed region has floors, side frames and deck beams at the frame spacing (dashed in the section), with their end brackets; change the framing of a region in the right panel, and the frame spacing in Settings.
  6. Buckling of plates and longitudinals under hull girder compression and the hull girder shear stress are checked too, in simplified form and marked as estimates. The plating is also checked as the flange of the web frames, where the frame's stress across the ship meets the hull girder stress along it (biaxial buckling). Lightening holes can be given per web frame member; they reduce its shear capacity.
  7. Change a thickness or a profile in the Structures table to see the effect at once. Click an element in the section for its checks.
  8. Section and 3D, above the view, switch between the half section of the region and a 3D view of the hull. Drag to turn, right-drag to pan, scroll to zoom; the buttons set standard views. In 3D the plates, longitudinals and primary members of every region follow the hull along its length, with the bulkheads; the selected region is in full colour, and clicking a region in 3D selects it. Hull, Structure and Bulkheads show or hide each part.
  9. Frame shows one web frame of the region as a beam model, as in Nauticus Hull 3D Beam: double bottom and double side as double skin beams, side web frame, floors, deck and tween transverses as girders with a plate flange, rigid ends at the knuckles. Pick a load case; tick Spaces to see how the case fills the spaces (and its draught) and Loads to see its loads on the beams, and pick the diagram: bending moment, shear, axial force or deformed shape. The Web frame tab lists each member with its forces, stresses and usage; change a girder there, or click a member for its properties and checks.
  10. Load cases sets the cases for the web frames: by default full load, ballast and tank test, read from the blocks (ballast, fuel, water and cargo tanks are liquid; other spaces carry their DBB mass on their floor). Change the draught, the sea, the green sea on deck, the head above the tank tops, the density or deck load of a space and which spaces are filled; add your own cases; untick a case to leave it out. Propose sizes the frames again for the cases.
  11. Report PDF makes a report of the whole ship: design and settings, every region with its section, web frame, tables and checks, the load cases, the method, the assumptions and the references. Save work keeps the design with your changes, settings and load cases in one .json file; Open DBB file opens it again.
  12. Learn, beside How to, opens eight short lessons on a barge: loads, shear force and bending moment; section properties; hull girder stresses; rule moments; plates and stiffeners under pressure; buckling; a web frame member by hand; holes and biaxial buckling. Work each by hand, type the answers and press Check (within 2% counts as right), or show the worked solution. Each lesson then compares the hand result with what the app computes for the same barge. The sliders under each figure change the conditions of that lesson (ballast, plating, length, spacing, holes); every change makes a new barge and clears the answers. New numbers gives another barge for practice; Open in the app loads it here.
  13. Drag the bar above the tables, or the row of tab names, to make the tables taller or shorter; double-click for the usual height.
  14. Settings change the spacing, the primary members and the tween deck load; Propose again makes a new proposal. Steel grade, service area, corrosion addition and web spacing come from the Structure tab of the DBB design.

Keys

  • Left and right arrows: previous and next region. Esc: clear the selection.

Limits

  • Longitudinal or transverse framing per region. Profiles are flat bars, unequal angles (L, EN 10056 sizes) and built T bars, drawn in 3D with their real web and flange; the lightest one that meets the rules is proposed. A rolled bulb (HP) table is not included yet.
  • Tank pressure is a head of water to the deck plus 0.76 m. Primary members use the general girder formula and are marked as an estimate.
  • Buckling is the classic simplified check (elastic buckling with the Johnson correction), with no lateral-torsional buckling; transverse frames use the general stiffener formula of the rules and brackets an estimated form; the shear stress is taken at the neutral axis only. All are marked as estimates.
  • One section and one web frame per region. The web frame is a plane beam model of the port half, not a finite element model: effective flanges (the web spacing, at most 0.3 of the member length), rigid ends and supports are assumptions and can move the stresses by about 20%. Its loads come from the load cases: sea pressure at the case draught, green sea on the weather deck, liquid heads to the tank top plus the head above it, and the DBB mass of dry spaces on their floor. No accelerations of the tank contents, and the half model cannot take a tank full on one side only. The equivalent stress limit 180 f1 and the minimum web thickness are assumed. Cut-outs only as round lightening holes in the web frames (shear area times 1 − d / h); no fatigue or torsion.
  • Where the plating, as the flange of a web frame, would buckle under the frame stress and the hull girder stress together, the proposal thickens the plating. Full-breadth tanks in the tank test drive most of this; a real design would often add buckling stiffeners or a centreline girder instead.
  • For educational use only: for learning and comparing concepts, not for the design, approval or construction of any ship, or any safety-critical decision.

Structure from DBB proposes the main longitudinal structure of a ship from its Design Building Block arrangement and checks it element by element. It reads the regions, the inner bottom, the inner side and the tween decks from the blocks of a DBB design, draws each section on the real hull, and sizes plates, longitudinals or transverse frames and primary members to the rules, with the hull girder section modulus, shear and buckling checked region by region. The transverse web frame of each region is analysed as a beam model, in the manner of the 3D Beam program of Nauticus Hull, and its girders sized from the computed forces. Parts of it, the barge example, the lessons, the moment distributions, the buckling and the plating as flange of the web frames, are based on the compendium Strukturdesign av skip by Arne Jan Sollied (Høgskolen i Ålesund, 2009). It is a prototype for the Structure tab of the Ship Design Building Block Editor and runs the editor's own core.

Background

It follows the Hull Scantlings Design Assistant, made in 2018 by Olivia Chaves in her master thesis in Ship Design at NTNU, supervised by Henrique Gaspar and Henning Borgen, and presented at ICSOS 2018. That app was a simplified, open scantling tool: a knowledge base of rules kept apart from the structure, regions along the ship with their own sections, every fifth longitudinal a primary member, the smallest profile that meets the requirement, instant green and red feedback, a log of checked rules on every element, and weight, steel cost and welding from the elements.

This version keeps those ideas and adds what the blocks know: the sections come from the hull and the blocks instead of a library of four shapes, the regions from the bulkheads in the arrangement, and the local loads and rules from the DNV 2015 rules already used in the DBB Structure tab. Each rule is one entry with its reference, so more rules can be added later. Three errors of the 2018 code were corrected on the way: one pressure applied to every structure, the centre keel counted twice, and the wave coefficient 0.0856 L used above 90 m.

User manual

The user manual (PDF) explains the method step by step: how the blocks are read, the longitudinal structure, the web frames and load cases, the examples, the lessons, the assumptions and the limitations, with exercises for students and the symbols used.

Learn the basics

The lessons under Learn are inspired by the compendium Strukturdesign av skip by Arne Jan Sollied (Høgskolen i Ålesund, 2009). Its barge example, the hand calculation of the shear force and bending moment of a box barge with ballast at the ends, is the barge of the lessons and the first example of the app. The compendium also gave the rule distributions of the moments along the length, the buckling with the Johnson correction, the interaction formula for plating loaded both ways and the treatment of holes in webs. The text, the figures and the numbers of the lessons are written for this app.
